extracted.intended_audience: journalists, reporters, editors and journalism students
extracted.subtask_description: A concise checklist for journalists on how to attribute information, avoid plagiarism, and be transparent about sources when producing news stories (especially for web publishing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid plagiarism / credit others correctly
rubrics_metrics.description: If you use someone else’s work, ideas, or words without saying where they came from, it is called plagiarism. This is a serious offence that can end your career.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Master news attribution and referencing to ensure reporting is accurate, credible, and avoids plagiarism. The checklist is intended to help credit others correctly and maintain integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify the source of every fact
rubrics_metrics.description: Always tell your audience where you got your information. If you did not see it or hear it yourself, you must name the person, document, or organisation that provided the details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make clear the provenance of every non‑firsthand fact so readers can judge reliability; name the specific person, document, or organisation rather than leaving provenance vague.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use direct quotes sparingly and accurately
rubrics_metrics.description: If you use the exact words of a source, you must make it clear that they are not your own words. Ensure the wording is 100% accurate and attributed to the specific speaker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve direct quotation for when the exact phrasing matters; check quotes for verbatim accuracy and clearly attribute them to the correct speaker. See related guidance on the power of quotes in journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribute information from other media outlets
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are following a story that another news outlet broke first, you must credit them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use explicit attributions such as “as reported by the xxxx” or “according to a report in xxxx” to acknowledge where a story originated and avoid implying you broke it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyperlink to original documents when publishing on the web
rubrics_metrics.description: When writing for the web, provide a direct link to the report, study, or article you are referencing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Linking allows readers to check the facts themselves and builds trust. Provide direct links to primary documents, reports, studies or the original article being referenced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish background/common knowledge from sourced claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Common knowledge, such as the date of a public holiday, does not always need a source. However, any specific claim, opinion, or new discovery must have a clear trail back to the source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether a fact is widely known vs. a specific claim that requires sourcing; when in doubt, provide the source so the reader can verify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check and respect embargo rules
rubrics_metrics.description: If a source gives you information but asks you to wait until a certain time to publish it, respect that request.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Breaking an embargo can damage your reputation and relationships with sources. Verify embargo terms and confirm with the source if unclear before publishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be transparent about your research sources
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have used a news/press release or a news agency report as the basis of your story, it is good practice to mention this.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosing that a story is based on a press release or agency report shows openness about how the news was gathered and helps readers assess provenance and potential bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never copy and paste others' text
rubrics_metrics.description: Never copy text from the internet and present it as your own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if you are in a rush, always rewrite information in your own words while still crediting the original source for the facts. Direct copying risks plagiarism and professional consequences.
